content: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) is a chronic lung disease that primarily affects preterm infants who require respiratory support during the early days of life. It is a significant complication, with more than 30% of infants born at less than 27 weeks of gestation developing BPD. Mechanical ventilation is recognized as one of the primary contributors to the development of BPD. To mitigate lung injury in preterm infants with respiratory distress, alternative ventilation methods and non-invasive respiratory support strategies have been explored. These include nasal continuous positive airway pressure (NCPAP) and nasal intermittent positive pressure ventilation, which aim to avoid endotracheal intubation and protect the immature lungs of preterm infants. Despite these efforts, many preterm infants still require mechanical ventilation via an endotracheal tube due to worsening respiratory insufficiency. Evidence from recent studies indicates that 52% to 59% of preterm infants between 26 and 29 weeks of gestation initially managed with NCPAP in the delivery room eventually required intubation and mechanical ventilation during the neonatal period. Furthermore, 45% of infants receiving NCPAP required intubation and ventilation within the first week of life. While research has focused on non-invasive strategies, the benefits and safety of invasive ventilation techniques and various ventilation modes remain unclear. BPD, first described by Northway in 1967, is characterized by radiological, clinical, and histological changes in the lungs of preterm infants with respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) who are treated with oxygen and mechanical ventilation. Infants with BPD face an increased risk of mortality and long-term complications, including pulmonary and neurodevelopmental morbidities. These children are more likely to experience developmental delays, cognitive impairments, and language deficits compared to those without BPD. Additionally, they have higher rates of hospital readmission during the first year of life. Historically, classical BPD was defined by inflammation, necrotizing bronchiolitis, and interstitial fibrosis, which impaired oxygen exchange in the alveoli. This form of BPD was observed in infants who required intermittent positive pressure ventilation during the first week of life and exhibited respiratory disease symptoms at 28 days of age or older. However, as neonatal care has advanced, including the use of pulmonary surfactant replacement therapy and less aggressive ventilation techniques, the presentation of BPD has evolved. The new BPD is now more commonly observed in extremely preterm infants (<30 weeks gestation or <1000 g birth weight) who survive due to improved neonatal care. This form is characterized by uniformly dilated alveoli with thin septa and minimal interstitial fibrosis. The incidence of BPD is inversely related to birth weight. For example, it occurs in 51% of infants weighing 501–750 g, 34% of those weighing 751–1000 g, 15% of those weighing 1001–1250 g, and 6% of those weighing 1251–1500 g. While trends in developed countries show a decline in classical BPD and a rise in new BPD, data from middle-income countries, such as those in Latin America, are less comprehensive. Studies in these regions indicate that BPD remains a significant cause of morbidity and chronic disease among preterm infants, with an incidence of 24% in infants weighing 1000–1500 g. The lack of a uniform definition of BPD has contributed to variability in reported incidence rates worldwide, ranging from 19% to 58%. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) consensus definition, which considers gestational age at birth and the fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) required to maintain adequate oxygen saturation, is now widely used in research. Using this definition, a study of very low birth weight infants found that 30% met the criteria for moderate BPD, while 16% met the criteria for severe BPD. The management of respiratory distress in preterm infants during the first hours and days of life is critical for minimizing lung damage and improving outcomes. Assisted mechanical ventilation can be delivered through conventional mechanical ventilation (CMV) or high-frequency ventilation (HFV). CMV involves intermittent positive mandatory ventilation via an endotracheal tube and can be pressureor volume-targeted. Commonly used CMV modes include assist/control ventilation, synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation, pressure support ventilation, and volume-targeted ventilation. HFV, on the other hand, uses very high respiratory rates (>240 breaths per minute) and small tidal volumes, with techniques such as high-frequency oscillatory ventilation and high-frequency jet ventilation. While synchronized ventilation modes have been studied primarily during the weaning phase of RDS, high-frequency techniques have been explored as rescue treatments for infants who fail initial CMV. However, evidence on the effects of invasive ventilation strategies during the early treatment of RDS in preterm infants remains limited and inconclusive for many critical outcomes. Given that mechanical ventilation is a major contributor to BPD, lung-protective ventilation strategies and efforts to minimize the duration of mechanical ventilation are expected to reduce the incidence of BPD. Despite advancements in non-invasive respiratory support, many preterm infants still require invasive mechanical ventilation. Research comparing different invasive ventilation strategies has yielded extensive but heterogeneous evidence, with variations in patient characteristics, baseline risks, and ventilation settings across studies. It remains unclear whether one approach is superior to others in improving clinical outcomes for preterm infants with respiratory distress. To address this gap, a systematic overview of Cochrane and non-Cochrane systematic reviews and randomized controlled trials (RCTs) will be conducted. This overview will assess the quality of evidence on the effects of invasive ventilation strategies on BPD and other critical neonatal outcomes using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. The findings will help clinicians make informed decisions about treatment options for preterm infants with respiratory distress and guide future research in this field.
